title: DynamoDB Deep Dive
description: Explore DynamoDB's partition management, adaptive capacity, consistent hashing, and how it achieves single-digit millisecond latency at any scale.

segments.text: Amazon DynamoDB handles ten trillion requests per day with single-digit millisecond latency. It is the quintessential NoSQL database. Let's understand the engineering that makes this possible.

DynamoDB automatically partitions your table by the partition key. It uses consistent hashing to map keys to partitions. As your table grows, partitions split automatically. You never manage shards manually.

Each partition stores up to ten gigabytes and handles up to three thousand read capacity units or one thousand write capacity units. When a partition exceeds these limits, DynamoDB splits it into two child partitions.

The classic problem: hot partitions. If one partition key gets disproportionate traffic, that partition becomes a bottleneck while others sit idle. Early DynamoDB throttled hot partitions aggressively.
Think about how you would solve this.
segments.thought_prompt: You provisioned 10,000 WCU total, but one partition needs 5,000. The partition limit is 1,000. How would you redistribute capacity?

segments.text: Adaptive capacity. DynamoDB now automatically reallocates unused capacity from cool partitions to hot ones. If your table has headroom, the hot partition borrows from others. No manual intervention needed.

DynamoDB also provides burst capacity. Unused throughput is saved as burst credits for up to five minutes. When a sudden spike hits, the table draws from these credits before throttling. Smooths out bursty workloads.

On-demand mode eliminates capacity planning entirely. DynamoDB auto-scales to match your workload. You pay per request. Perfect for unpredictable traffic, but two to seven times more expensive than well-tuned provisioned mode.

Global tables provide multi-region replication with last-writer-wins conflict resolution. Writes in any region replicate asynchronously to all others. Read latency is local, but conflicts are resolved with wall-clock timestamps.

DynamoDB Accelerator, DAX, is an in-memory cache sitting in front of DynamoDB. It reduces read latency from single-digit milliseconds to microseconds. Write-through caching ensures consistency. Ideal for read-heavy workloads.

segments.thought_prompt: Your application has a table with 500 million items and a partition key that is user_id. 1% of users generate 50% of traffic. How would you design the key schema?

segments.text: Add a random suffix to scatter hot users across partitions, then use a scatter-gather pattern for reads. Or use a composite sort key for time-series access. DynamoDB rewards good key design and punishes bad ones. Master the partition key, and you master DynamoDB.
